catalog_locator: §6 Tone, printed p. 26 (PDF p. 27) and §6.1 Tone Inventory, printed p. 27 (PDF p. 28); page images, (renders)
catalog_quote: Tone is an indispensible part of the sound system of Ngomba and is just as important as the segmentals. There are many lexical items which are distinguished only by tone, e.g., [káŋ] 'plate' and [kàŋ] 'squirrel'. Tone is essential not only because it carries a high lexical load, but also because of its grammatical functions. ... 6.1 Tone Inventory. Ngomba has two basic tones : 1. H (HIGH) 2. L (LOW). Phonetically one also finds a M (MID) tone, but I believe this to be a downstepped High. Downstep may be defined as a shift downward in the tone register, i.e. in the range of the tones, and is generally thought to be caused by a floating Low tone. ... There are two types of Low tones. As in other grassfields languages (e.g. Yemba) one may distinguish phrase-finally between a non-falling or level Low (L°) and a L which falls in this position. ... Phonetically one finds the contours : F, a high-low falling tone, R a low-high rising tone and RF a rise-fall. One may view these as sequences of basic tones, as is common in African languages.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given: the description treats Ngomba as a two-tone language (H, L, with downstep and phonetic contours) and never mentions stress, accent or prominence. The section headed 'Prosodies' (§4.2) concerns palatalization, labialization and length, not stress. The same holds for Ngouagna 1988 (p. 17: 'Le parler njinda est une langue à tons' — the Njinda variety is a tone language; six phonetic tone levels, four tonemes) and for Satre 2010 (SAL 39(1): 36, two basic tones L and H).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None; no stress statement exists to have exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (lexical roots mostly monosyllabic, CV(C) with 'echo vowel' in long closed syllables) plus grammatical/concord tone at phrase level; Satre also distinguishes phrase-final falling L from level L°. Nothing on stress at word or phrase level.
new_statements.identity_note: Both phonologies describe the Bamendjinda (Njinda) village variety, the SIL reference dialect of Ngomba (ALCAM 940); the other varieties are Bamesso, Bamenkoumbo, Babete and Bamendjo. Ngouagna 1988 names his object 'le parler njinda' and treats it as part of 'l'aire ngomba'. No separate glottocode for the Bamendjinda variety; it falls under ngom1272. Not to be confused with Ngombale [nla] (ngom1271), a different Bamileke language.

new_statements.quote: This is accomplished in Ngomba by an intricate system of segmental AUXes, particles, and affixes as well as tonal markers. As tense-related affixes occur at a certain position in the verb phrase, they often "land" on various AUXes rather than the main verb, thus substantiating the claim that tense/aspect and negation marking are an operation on the verb phrase level rather than on the verb itself. This 'hopping around' of an affix (and accompanying tonal changes) is illustrated in the P2 examples (6-8) below. The P2 'Yesterday Past' is marked by a combination of an affix - high tone nasal prefix - and a 'super low' tone on the verb root that overrides the lexical tone.
new_statements.citation: Satre, Scott Alan. 2004. Structure of the Verb Phrase in Ngomba. Yaoundé: MINREST & SIL. iii+32 pp.
new_statements.locator: §3.1.1 Tense/aspect/negation markers, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 12), verified against the page image; also p. 26 (PDF p. 30) on downstep

Rendered PDF p. 12 at 120 dpi and read the page image: the quoted passage sits in §3.1.1 'Tense/aspect/negation markers in the structure of the verb phrase' exactly as quoted, from 'This is accomplished in Ngomba by an intricate system of segmental AUXes, particles, and affixes as well as tonal markers' through 'a "super low" tone on the verb root that' (page break) 'overrides the lexical tone' at the top of printed p. 9. Rendered PDF p. 30 (printed p. 26) and confirmed 'the downstep is between the first and second mora of complement clause'. Whole-text a full-text search for stress/accent the scanned for stress/accen…
new_statements.relation_note: Silent on stress in so many words, but corroborates the existing Satre 1997 statement (tone language, no stress statement): tone is lexical and grammatical, and the same author again describes word prosody only in terms of tone, downstep and moras. Adds nothing about placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper is a syntax description (constituent order, agreement, verb chains, objects and complements, adjuncts) with no phonology or prosody section. It presupposes lexical tone on verb and noun roots (H vs L roots, 'overrides the lexical tone', downstep, super-low grammatical tone for P2) and never mentions word stress, accent or prominence; the only 'accent' hits in the whole scanned are the orthographic 'grave accent' that marks the P2 tense (pp. 8-9, fn. 22 p. 10).
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress statement at all); p. 26 notes that a downstep may fall 'between the first and second mora' of a long-syllable subject noun, i.e., the paper treats moras/tone register, not stress
new_statements.identity_note: Satre 2004 names no village; p. 1 places Ngomba on the Bamileke plateau, West Province, Cameroon, and p. 23 draws some examples from the Bird & Bell 2001 Ngomba tone-data CD. Satre 1997 (the existing statement) uses Bamendjinda data, Satre 2002 Bamendjinda and Bamesso, Ngouagna 1988 the Njinda (Bamendjinda) variety; no dialect disagreement arises because no source states a stress rule.
